title: Sold out, but 2,000 people still ordered it
brief: A restaurant marks butter chicken as out of stock on its tablet. For the next 90 seconds, 2,000 people still manage to order it. The menu cache TTL is 60 seconds. The search index refreshes every 30 seconds. Explain where the 90 seconds come from, and get the delay under 5 seconds without hammering the database.
insight: The stale windows stack: the tablet writes to the primary database; the app reads the menu from a cache with a 60 s TTL; the cache refills from the search index, which only refreshes every 30 s. Worst case 60 + 30 = 90 s. The fix is event-driven, not shorter TTLs: on the stock change, write to the database and emit one event (via an outbox or change stream) that deletes or updates that one cache key and updates that one document in the search index. Short TTLs on everything would hammer the database. Also make order placement check availability against the source of truth (or an atomic availability flag in Redis) so stale browse pages cannot create orders. Coalesce refills for the one invalidated key so 2,000 readers cause one database read, not 2,000. Do not flush the whole cache.

title: 100 items, 140 orders
brief: A flash sale lists 100 units of a console. 50,000 people press Buy in the first 10 seconds. Afterwards the orders table has 140 confirmed orders. The stock check reads the count, compares it to zero, then writes the order and decrements in a separate statement.
insight: Check-then-act race between concurrent requests. The fix is an atomic conditional decrement (UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0 and check the affected row count, or Redis DECR / a Lua script) so the check and the change are one operation. Locking the whole table or running one server only would not scale. For 50,000 requests for 100 items, put a cheap gate in front (Redis counter or a queue) so most requests are rejected without touching the database. Reserve stock with an expiry, then confirm after payment. Verify with a load test that confirmed orders never exceed stock.

title: The customer was charged twice
brief: A customer taps Pay on a slow mobile connection. The request times out in the app, the app retries automatically, and the card is charged twice. The payment service calls an external payment processor and then writes the result to its own database.
insight: A timeout does not tell the client whether the server did the work, so retries are normal and the server must make them safe. Use an idempotency key generated by the client per payment attempt, stored with a unique constraint along with the result, and pass the same key to the processor. A repeated request with the same key returns the stored result instead of charging again. Disabling the button or removing retries does not fix it (network retries and double taps still happen). Also handle the crash between 'processor charged' and 'we saved the result' by reconciling against the processor by key.

title: The database falls over at exactly 00:00
brief: A popular profile page is cached in Redis for 1 hour. Every time its key expires, the database CPU jumps to 100% for a few seconds and p99 latency climbs from 40 ms to 4 s. Thousands of requests per second ask for that profile.
insight: Cache stampede (thundering herd): when the hot key expires, every concurrent request misses and recomputes the same value against the database. Fixes: single flight / request coalescing or a short-lived lock so one request refills while others wait or serve the stale value; stale-while-revalidate or refresh-ahead before expiry; add random jitter to TTLs so many keys do not expire together. Raising the TTL only delays the problem, and adding database replicas treats the symptom.

title: Every user got the email twice
brief: A background worker sends an order confirmation email, then marks the job done. During a deploy the worker is killed after it sent the email but before it marked the job done. After restart, every in-flight job runs again and customers get two emails.
insight: The queue delivers at least once: an unacknowledged job is redelivered after a crash, so the handler must be idempotent. Record a unique 'email sent' marker per (order, template) before or atomically with sending and skip if present; use the provider's idempotency key if it has one. Exactly-once delivery is not something to rely on. Also shut workers down gracefully (finish or hand back jobs on SIGTERM) to reduce, not remove, duplicates. Removing retries would lose emails.

title: One shard is on fire
brief: A social app shards its posts table by user_id across 8 database servers. When one celebrity with 20 million followers posts, the shard holding that user hits 100% CPU while the other seven sit at 10%. Adding more shards did not help.
insight: Hot key / hot partition: hashing spreads keys evenly, but one key carries a disproportionate share of traffic, so more shards do not help. Fixes: cache the hot reads (the celebrity's posts are read-heavy and nearly immutable) in a CDN or Redis; replicate or add read replicas for that shard; for write or counter hot spots, split the key (append a random suffix 0..N and aggregate on read); handle celebrities differently from normal users (fan-out on read for them). Re-sharding by a different key does not remove a single hot key.

title: The rate limit allows five times too much
brief: An API promises 100 requests per minute per user. It runs on 5 identical servers behind a load balancer, each with an in-memory counter. Customers measure about 500 requests per minute getting through, and the database is overloaded.
insight: Each server counts only the requests it sees, so the effective limit is 5 x 100. Counters must be shared: a central store such as Redis with an atomic INCR plus expiry (fixed window), or an atomic Lua script implementing a token bucket or sliding window. Sticky sessions would reduce but not guarantee correctness and unbalance load. Dividing the limit by the number of servers breaks when servers scale or traffic is uneven. Consider failure mode (fail open vs fail closed if Redis is down) and per-request latency of the shared store.

title: The leaderboard page gets slower every week
brief: A game shows the top 100 players and each player's own rank. The query is SELECT ... ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 100 plus SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE score > ? for the rank. With 50 million players the page takes 6 seconds, and it is slower each week.
insight: Sorting and counting over the whole table per request is O(n) or O(n log n) per request. A composite or descending index on score helps the top 100 but rank still needs counting. A sorted set in Redis (ZADD, ZREVRANGE for the top N, ZREVRANK for a player's rank) answers both in O(log n) and is updated as scores change; the database remains the system of record. Caching the page for a few seconds helps further. Adding read replicas alone does not change the complexity. Mention rebuild from the database if Redis is lost and handling ties.

title: I saved my profile, and it shows the old one
brief: A user changes their display name and is redirected to their profile page, which shows the old name. A refresh a few seconds later shows the new one. Writes go to the primary database; reads are load balanced across three replicas.
insight: Replication lag: the read after the write hit a replica that had not yet applied the change. The guarantee needed is read-your-writes for the user who wrote. Fixes: route that user's reads to the primary for a short window after a write (a timestamp or session flag), or read from a replica only if it has caught up to the write's log position, or return the updated object in the write response and render from it. Sending all reads to the primary removes the benefit of replicas. Synchronous replication to all replicas costs write latency and availability. Other users seeing the old name briefly is acceptable.

title: Chat messages arrive out of order after reconnecting
brief: A chat app delivers messages over WebSockets. When a phone loses signal and reconnects, the conversation shows some messages twice and some in the wrong order. The server assigns no sequence numbers and the client appends whatever arrives.
insight: The client cannot tell what it has already seen or what order messages happened in, and reconnects replay or interleave deliveries. Give each message a per-conversation monotonically increasing sequence number (or a server-assigned ordered id) at write time; the client tracks the last sequence it has applied, dedupes by message id, and on reconnect asks the server for everything after its last sequence number. Sorting by client timestamp is unreliable because of clock skew. Making the server resend everything is wasteful. The database is the source of truth; the socket is only a fast path.

title: Checkout returns 502s while the database CPU is only 8%
brief: After autoscaling from 40 to 240 API pods during a TV campaign, checkout traffic rises to 12,000 requests/minute. p95 latency jumps to 22 seconds and then the load balancer emits 502s, but PostgreSQL CPU stays under 10% and disk I/O is flat. Database logs show thousands of short-lived sessions and many clients waiting to acquire a connection.
insight: The root cause is connection exhaustion: each pod owns a pool of 50 connections, so the fleet can demand 12,000 connections against a database configured for 600. The fix is to budget connections globally, shrink per-pod pools, add PgBouncer/RDS Proxy where appropriate, and make autoscaling respect the database connection budget. Do not simply raise max_connections; PostgreSQL spends more memory and scheduler time per backend and can get slower. The trade-off is that transaction pooling can break session state, prepared statements, temp tables, and LISTEN/NOTIFY unless the application is adjusted.

title: A few users download invoices that belong to someone else
brief: Support receives 37 reports in an hour from users seeing another customer's PDF invoice from /api/invoices/latest. The endpoint sits behind a CDN with a 7-day default TTL and receives about 900 requests/second at peak. The application authenticates correctly, but the CDN cache key is only the URL path and query string.
insight: The root cause is caching authenticated content without varying the cache by user identity, cookie, or Authorization header. The fix is to mark account-specific responses Cache-Control: private or no-store, use per-user signed URLs where caching is needed, add Vary: Authorization/Cookie only when safe, and purge already-cached objects. Do not fix this by disabling the CDN for the whole site without analysis; static and public content can remain cached. The trade-off is lower cache hit rate for personalized data versus correctness and privacy.

title: Deleted project names stay unavailable for 30 minutes
brief: Users delete a project and immediately try to recreate it with the same slug, but the API returns 409 Conflict for about 30 minutes. The uniqueness row is removed from MySQL within 40 ms, and direct database checks show the slug is free. The availability endpoint is cached in Redis with a 1,800-second TTL and handles 4,000 checks/second during onboarding.
insight: The root cause is an existence/negative-result cache that is not invalidated on delete or rename. The fix is to invalidate or update the cache in the same code path as the write, use shorter TTLs for mutable availability checks, and still rely on the database unique constraint for final enforcement. Do not remove the unique constraint and trust the cache; caches are advisory and can be stale. The trade-off is more cache churn and database reads versus better user-visible freshness.

title: Thumbnail generation is six hours behind with workers at 100%
brief: A new import path adds 2 million images in 20 minutes, and the thumbnail queue grows from 5,000 to 1.4 million messages. Workers process normal JPEGs in 120 ms, but a small number of 400 MB TIFFs time out after the 30-second visibility timeout and are retried indefinitely. The queue has no dead-letter queue and only one priority class.
insight: The root cause is poison messages consuming worker capacity and repeatedly reappearing before successful work can drain. The fix is to set max receive counts, send failed jobs to a DLQ, enforce input size/type limits before enqueueing, make processing idempotent, and use backoff or separate queues for expensive media. Do not just add more workers; they will spend more money retrying the same impossible jobs. The trade-off is that some jobs become delayed or require manual remediation, but the rest of the system continues making progress.

title: Wallet balances occasionally go negative during busy hours
brief: A prepaid wallet service handles about 300 debit requests/second for the same popular merchant accounts. Twice a day, balances that started with $20 end up at -$5 or -$10 even though each debit checks the current balance first. The database uses READ COMMITTED isolation and the code performs SELECT balance, then UPDATE balance in two separate statements.
insight: The root cause is a lost-update race: concurrent transactions read the same balance and both decide funds are available. The fix is an atomic conditional update such as UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ? AND balance >= ?, or a row lock/serializable transaction around the balance mutation. Do not use an in-process mutex because it fails across pods and during restarts. The trade-off is increased contention on hot wallet rows; if that becomes limiting, use ledger entries plus reserved balances or partition by account semantics, not by pretending the race is acceptable.

title: Password reset links fail once, then work a few seconds later
brief: About 4% of password reset attempts return invalid_token on the first click, but succeed if the user clicks again 5 to 10 seconds later. The reset token is written to the primary database, while validation reads from a read replica. During evening traffic the replica lag is normally 2 seconds and sometimes spikes to 12 seconds.
insight: The root cause is reading a freshly written token from an asynchronously replicated replica that has not caught up. The fix is to validate security-sensitive freshly created tokens on the primary, route by a read-your-writes consistency token, or wait for a specific replica LSN before reading. Do not increase token TTL as the main fix; the problem is visibility, not expiration. The trade-off is more primary read load or added routing complexity in exchange for correct user flows.

title: New posts do not appear in search for several minutes
brief: The product promises searchable posts within 10 seconds, but during peak publishing 15,000 posts/minute, new posts appear in timelines immediately and in search 3 to 8 minutes later. Elasticsearch refresh_interval is 60 seconds, and bulk indexing workers are also backlogged by 500,000 documents. Users can find the post by direct URL but not by search query.
insight: The root cause is eventual consistency in the search indexing pipeline plus bulk backlog, not missing database writes. The fix is to size and monitor the indexer queue, use refresh policies selectively for user-critical documents, expose pending-index state, and optionally merge database results for the author's own recent posts. Do not set refresh_interval to 1 ms globally; it will destroy indexing throughput and segment efficiency. The trade-off is between search freshness, indexing cost, and query performance.

title: One provider sends 80,000 signups without tripping the IP limit
brief: Abuse traffic creates 80,000 accounts in 25 minutes from a single hosting provider. The per-IP limit is 5 signups/hour, and logs show every request using a different IPv6 /128 address within a few /64 prefixes. Email verification, CAPTCHA, and device checks are only applied after account creation.
insight: The root cause is rate limiting on individual IPv6 addresses, which attackers can rotate cheaply within a prefix. The fix is to aggregate IPv6 limits at /64 or provider-specific prefix sizes, combine IP limits with account, device, ASN, and payment/email reputation signals, and move expensive verification before account creation when risk is high. Do not block the entire ISP or all IPv6 traffic by default; that creates large false positives. The trade-off is stricter abuse control versus potentially throttling legitimate users behind shared infrastructure.

title: WebSocket gateways restart every five minutes in synchronized waves
brief: The realtime fleet holds about 180,000 concurrent WebSocket connections. Every five minutes, gateway CPU jumps to 100%, connection attempts spike to 70,000/second, and several pods fail liveness checks. The load balancer idle timeout is 300 seconds, while clients send heartbeats every 10 minutes and reconnect immediately with no jitter.
insight: The root cause is synchronized disconnects caused by the load balancer closing idle connections, followed by an unjittered reconnect storm. The fix is to send ping/pong heartbeats more frequently than the idle timeout, add exponential backoff with jitter on reconnect, drain connections during deploys, and rate-limit handshakes. Do not only double gateway capacity; the storm can grow with the client population. The trade-off is more steady heartbeat traffic in exchange for avoiding catastrophic bursts.

title: Refunds stay pending even after support retries them
brief: Support retries failed refunds from an admin tool, but 11% remain pending for more than 24 hours. The tool reuses the original payment idempotency key for every refund attempt, even when the requested amount or reason changes. The payment processor returns the cached first 202 Accepted response for that key and never creates a new refund operation.
insight: The root cause is using the wrong idempotency scope: the capture/payment key is reused for distinct refund operations. The fix is to model refunds as their own state-machine records, generate one stable idempotency key per semantic refund request, persist processor IDs, and reconcile via webhooks and polling. Do not remove idempotency from retries; that risks duplicate refunds on timeouts. The trade-off is more bookkeeping and reconciliation logic, but retries become safe and auditable.

title: The canary is green, then the full release produces 500s
brief: A new version is canaried to 5% of web traffic for 30 minutes with no visible errors. After full rollout, error rate jumps to 18% because background workers still on the old version read rows written by the new version. The release changed a column from nullable to required and started writing a new enum value that old workers do not recognize.
insight: The root cause is a non-backward-compatible deploy across a mixed-version fleet that includes workers not covered by the canary. The fix is an expand-and-contract migration: add fields and enum values compatibly, deploy readers that tolerate both formats, backfill, then enforce constraints and remove old code after all producers/consumers are upgraded. Do not rely on fast rollback after an incompatible data write; old code may already be unable to read the new data. The trade-off is slower multi-step releases, but safe rollouts and rollbacks.

title: All dashboards are green while checkout is unusable
brief: For 17 minutes, users cannot complete checkout, but the main service dashboard shows 99.98% availability. The only alerting SLI is GET /health returning 200, and aggregate API latency is dominated by cheap read endpoints. Checkout POST /checkout errors at 35%, but it is only 1.5% of total request volume.
insight: The root cause is observability that measures infrastructure liveness and aggregate averages instead of user-critical behavior. The fix is to define SLIs per critical journey, including checkout success rate and latency, add synthetic transactions, and alert on burn rates for those SLIs. Do not page on CPU or generic health checks alone; they can be green during real user outages. The trade-off is more instrumentation and alert tuning to avoid noise, but incidents become detectable by user impact.

title: EU users are logged out during a US region failover
brief: A planned US-east failover shifts authentication traffic to EU-west for 20 minutes. About 1.2 million EU users are forced to log in again, and 9% cannot log in until the failover ends. Session state is stored in a regional Redis cluster with a 12-hour TTL, while signing keys and session revocation lists are not replicated consistently.
insight: The root cause is treating session state and auth key material as regional while routing users across regions. The fix is to replicate session/revocation data with defined consistency, use stateless tokens with globally distributed keys where appropriate, or keep users pinned to a region that owns their sessions. Do not depend on DNS stickiness alone; failover and mobile networks break that assumption. The trade-off is between fast revocation and global availability: fully stateless tokens are resilient but harder to revoke immediately.

title: Uploads complete successfully, but downloads are zero bytes
brief: Roughly 0.6% of direct-to-storage uploads appear successful in the UI but download as 0-byte files. Clients call the application callback after receiving a presigned URL, and the app marks the file complete before verifying the object. Network traces show some mobile clients abort after creating the object key but before sending the 20 to 80 MB payload.
insight: The root cause is trusting the client callback instead of verifying that the storage object exists with the expected size and checksum. The fix is to finalize uploads only after a storage completion event or HEAD check confirms content length, checksum/ETag, and multipart completion, then write the database row as complete. Do not let clients choose arbitrary final object state. The trade-off is slightly delayed availability and more storage API calls, but file metadata matches reality.

title: The daily digest job runs 32 times every morning
brief: At 08:00 UTC, users receive 32 digest rows in their activity history, though email sending is suppressed after the first. The service was scaled from 4 to 32 pods, and each pod runs the same in-process cron scheduler. The job takes about 11 minutes and has no distributed lock or idempotent output key.
insight: The root cause is running a singleton scheduled task independently in every replica. The fix is to use an external scheduler, leader election with leases, or a durable job queue with a unique job key, and make the job idempotent by writing digest rows with a deterministic uniqueness constraint. Do not add random sleep and hope only one pod wins; races remain during restarts and partitions. The trade-off is adding coordination infrastructure, but scheduled work becomes reliable under scaling.

title: Users are logged out after six minutes instead of six hours
brief: A session-service refactor changes TTL configuration from integer seconds to a duration string. The intended 6-hour TTL is deployed as 360 seconds for Redis session keys, affecting all new logins at about 9,000/minute. Existing sessions remain valid, so the issue appears gradually over the first hour.
insight: The root cause is a time-unit mismatch in session TTL configuration. The fix is to use strongly typed duration parsing, reject ambiguous numeric values, add tests around expected TTLs, and monitor session key expirations after deploys. Do not set sessions to never expire as a quick fix; that creates security and storage problems. The trade-off is stricter configuration validation that may reject previously accepted values, but it prevents silent security regressions.

title: Older Android clients get 400s after the API release
brief: Within an hour of deploying v3.12 of the API, error rate for Android app versions older than 8.4 rises to 42%. The endpoint POST /orders/address now requires a new field, delivery_instructions, with no default. About 18% of active Android devices are on versions that cannot send the field for at least two weeks.
insight: The root cause is a backward-incompatible request contract change on an unversioned endpoint. The fix is to make new fields optional with server-side defaults, use explicit API versioning or capability negotiation, and deprecate old clients only after measuring adoption. Do not solve this by forcing an immediate mobile upgrade; app-store rollout and user behavior make that unreliable. The trade-off is keeping compatibility code longer, but mobile APIs must tolerate slow client upgrades.

title: The CDN bill quadruples overnight with the same traffic
brief: Daily CDN egress cost jumps from $4,800 to $19,000 while page views increase by only 3%. Cache hit ratio drops from 92% to 18% after a frontend SDK release. The SDK appends a millisecond timestamp query parameter to every image and script URL for tracing.
insight: The root cause is cache-key fragmentation from a high-cardinality query parameter. The fix is to configure the CDN to ignore or normalize non-content-affecting query parameters, move tracing data to headers or beacons, and use content-hashed asset URLs for cache busting. Do not buy more bandwidth or increase origin capacity as the primary response; the same bytes are being needlessly refetched. The trade-off is careful cache-key design so true variants, such as image size or locale, still remain distinct.

title: Month-end reports time out for large customers
brief: On the last day of the month, enterprise customers with more than 80 million transactions see the reports page time out after 60 seconds. The query filters by org_id, created_at range, and status, then sorts by created_at desc. The only relevant index is on status, so the database scans tens of millions of rows for common statuses.
insight: The root cause is an index that does not match the query's selectivity and ordering. The fix is a composite index such as (org_id, created_at DESC, status) or (org_id, status, created_at DESC) depending on cardinality and query shapes, possibly with covering columns or monthly partitioning. Do not add many single-column indexes and expect the planner to magically combine them efficiently for this workload. The trade-off is additional write amplification and storage, so index choices should be based on observed query patterns.

title: Read receipts lag by hours after the push provider slows down
brief: The read-receipt queue normally drains 25,000 jobs/second, but after a push provider starts returning 429s, backlog grows to 90 million jobs. Workers retry failed push jobs immediately and put them back at the front of the same queue. Cheap internal receipt writes are stuck behind third-party calls that are limited to 2,000/second.
insight: The root cause is retry amplification and head-of-line blocking between internal work and a rate-limited dependency. The fix is to separate queues by dependency and priority, apply token-bucket limits for the push provider, use exponential backoff with jitter, and move exhausted retries to a DLQ. Do not increase worker count; it will amplify 429s and starve useful work faster. The trade-off is that external notifications may be delayed, but core read-receipt state can remain current.

title: A tenant migration loses ten minutes of writes
brief: A 600 GB enterprise tenant is moved from shard 12 to shard 27 using a snapshot copy that takes 74 minutes. Routing is switched at 14:00, but writes that landed on shard 12 between 13:50 and 14:00 are missing on shard 27. The migration process copied a snapshot, replayed no change log, and did not block or dual-write during cutover.
insight: The root cause is a shard migration without a consistent cutover protocol for writes occurring after the snapshot. The fix is to use CDC/WAL catch-up, dual-write with verification, or briefly quiesce the tenant while copying the final delta, then switch routing with a versioned mapping. Do not rely on a filesystem or SQL snapshot alone for live tenants. The trade-off is added migration complexity or a short maintenance window versus preserving write correctness.

title: Deleted documents remain searchable for hours
brief: Users delete private documents from the database, but search still returns snippets for 2 to 6 hours. Deletes are performed in the API transaction, and a best-effort in-process call enqueues a search delete after commit. During deploy restarts, about 0.3% of those enqueue calls are lost.
insight: The root cause is a non-transactional side effect between the database delete and the search-index delete event. The fix is a transactional outbox or CDC stream that records delete tombstones in the same database transaction and guarantees indexer delivery with retries. Do not rely on periodic full reindexing as the only fix; it leaves privacy-sensitive stale results visible for too long. The trade-off is more pipeline infrastructure and tombstone handling, but search converges reliably.

title: One GraphQL query melts the API for everyone
brief: A customer dashboard sends a single GraphQL query with 7 nested levels: orgs, projects, issues, comments, authors, reactions, and attachments. At 150 requests/minute, database queries jump from 8,000/second to 220,000/second because each resolver performs its own SELECT. API CPU saturates and unrelated endpoints time out.
insight: The root cause is unbounded query complexity combined with N+1 resolver behavior. The fix is to enforce depth and cost limits, require pagination on list fields, batch and cache resolver loads with DataLoader-style mechanisms, and set per-tenant query budgets. Do not disable GraphQL entirely or only increase database size; the API must control the work a client can request. The trade-off is less client flexibility for pathological queries, but predictable capacity and fairness.

title: Alerts fire twenty minutes after users start seeing errors
brief: A regional outage causes 25% 5xx responses at 10:03, but the first page arrives at 10:24. Services buffer metrics locally for 60 seconds, the collector is overloaded and lags by 8 minutes, and the alert uses a 15-minute rolling average. Logs show the error spike immediately, but alerting is based only on delayed metrics.
insight: The root cause is an alert pipeline with too much ingestion delay and an overly slow detection window for acute failures. The fix is to monitor telemetry pipeline lag, alert on fast burn-rate windows, use direct black-box probes for critical paths, and keep a low-latency signal separate from bulk analytics. Do not simply lower every threshold; that increases noise without fixing delayed data. The trade-off is operating multiple signal paths, but pages arrive while the incident is still unfolding.

title: DNS failover sends all users to a region that cannot serve them
brief: A health check fails in us-east, so DNS shifts 100% of traffic to us-west within 60 seconds. The west region has only 25% warm capacity, its database replica is 23 minutes behind, and several feature-flag values were never replicated. Error rate rises from 12% to 68% after the automatic failover.
insight: The root cause is failover automation that checks source-region health but not target-region readiness, capacity, and replication lag. The fix is to gate failover on target health, replica lag, dependency readiness, and prewarmed capacity, and to practice partial traffic shifts with runbooks. Do not treat low DNS TTL as a disaster recovery plan by itself. The trade-off is that automatic failover may be slower or blocked, but it avoids failing into a worse state.

title: Product images disappear fifteen minutes after upload
brief: Sellers upload product images successfully, and the images render in the admin UI for a short time. After exactly 15 minutes, public product pages show broken images for about 40% of new listings. The application stored the presigned upload URL in the product record instead of the stable object key or CDN URL.
insight: The root cause is persisting a temporary presigned URL as if it were a permanent download URL. The fix is to store the object key and generate separate read URLs, either public CDN URLs for public images or short-lived signed download URLs for private content. Do not make the entire bucket public to hide the bug; access control should match object sensitivity. The trade-off is adding URL-generation logic, but storage identity and access policy stay separate.

title: Scheduled promotions start one hour late in one country
brief: A retailer schedules promotions for 09:00 local time in Europe/London, but on the daylight-saving transition weekend they start at 10:00 for 1.8 million users. The scheduler stores only a UTC timestamp computed at creation time and later clones schedules by adding 24 hours. The UI displays local time, so operators believe the schedule is correct.
insight: The root cause is treating recurring local-time business events as fixed UTC intervals across daylight-saving changes. The fix is to store the intended timezone and local wall-clock rule, compute each occurrence using a timezone database, and define behavior for nonexistent or repeated local times. Do not fix it with a one-off UTC offset; offsets change by region and date. The trade-off is more complex scheduling semantics, but promotions match user and business expectations.

title: Admins are stuck in a login loop for 24 hours
brief: After rotating signing keys, 60% of admin login attempts succeed and then immediately redirect back to login. API servers fetch JWKS with a 24-hour cache TTL, but the old key was removed from the key set immediately. Depending on which server handles the next request, the same token is accepted or rejected.
insight: The root cause is unsafe JWT key rotation without overlap between old and new verification keys and with long-lived JWKS caches. The fix is to publish new keys before use, sign with the new key only after caches can see it, keep old keys until all issued tokens expire plus cache TTL, and use kid to select keys. Do not disable signature verification or flush caches manually as the primary mechanism. The trade-off is carrying multiple active public keys for a period, which is normal for safe rotation.

title: Analytics counts drop to zero after a harmless schema change
brief: A producer release renames the event field userId to user_id and continues sending 120,000 events/second. The stream processor expects userId, treats missing values as anonymous, and drops anonymous events from customer dashboards. No alert fires because the Kafka topic volume is unchanged.
insight: The root cause is an incompatible event schema change with consumers that silently accept missing required fields. The fix is to use a schema registry or contract tests, make schema evolution backward compatible by emitting both fields during migration, and alert on semantic counters such as non-null user IDs. Do not coordinate a big-bang producer and consumer deploy; distributed rollouts are never perfectly simultaneous. The trade-off is temporary duplicate fields and stricter validation, but analytics remains continuous.

title: The read replica falls further behind every night
brief: Every night at 02:00, a BI query runs for 90 minutes on the read replica and replication lag grows from 3 seconds to more than 45 minutes. The primary continues writing 18,000 rows/second, and WAL replay on the replica slows while the long snapshot is active. Morning users see stale dashboards and occasional query cancellations.
insight: The root cause is mixing long-running analytics snapshots with a replica expected to provide fresh operational reads. The fix is to move BI to a dedicated analytics replica or warehouse, cap query duration, tune hot-standby conflict settings intentionally, and monitor replication lag as an SLO. Do not just scale the replica vertically; a single long snapshot can still interfere with replay and vacuum behavior. The trade-off is higher infrastructure cost or stricter BI limits in exchange for predictable freshness.
